# # Heart Rate Variability (HRV)

# NeuroKit2 is the most comprehensive package when it comes to HRV indices, and this example shows how to use NeuroKit2 to compute heart rate variability (HRV) indices in the time-, frequency-, and non-linear domain.
#
# For a comprehensive review of the most up-to-date HRV indices, a discussion of their significance in psychology, and a step-by-step guide for HRV analysis using **NeuroKit2**, the [Heart Rate Variability in Psychology: A Review of HRV Indices and an Analysis Tutorial](https://doi.org/10.3390/s21123998) paper is a good place to start. 

# ## Compute HRV features

# Load the NeuroKit package
import neurokit2 as nk

# Note: this cell is hidden using the "remove-input" tag
# Make bigger images
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# --- Offline input adaptation (environment-only; no scientific change) ---
# The original notebook relies on nk.data() fetching its example dataset from
# https://raw.githubusercontent.com/neuropsychology/NeuroKit/master/data/ .
# The exact dataset file is staged at /inputs/ so the offline reference can
# read identical bytes through the unchanged nk.data() code path.
_orig_pd_read_csv = nk.pd.read_csv


def _offline_read_csv(path, *args, **kwargs):
    _nk_data_prefix = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/neuropsychology/NeuroKit/master/data/"
    if isinstance(path, str) and path.startswith(_nk_data_prefix):
        return _orig_pd_read_csv("/inputs/" + path[len(_nk_data_prefix):], *args, **kwargs)
    return _orig_pd_read_csv(path, *args, **kwargs)


nk.pd.read_csv = _offline_read_csv


plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = [15, 5]
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 14

# ## Download Dataset

# First, let's download the resting rate data (sampled at 100Hz) using `nk.data()`.

data = nk.data("bio_resting_5min_100hz")
data.head()  # Print first 5 rows

# You can see that it consists of three different signals, pertaining to ECG, PPG (an alternative determinant of heart rate as compared to ECG), and RSP (respiration). Now, let's extract the ECG signal in the shape of a vector (i.e., a one-dimensional array), and find the peaks using [ecg_peaks()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/ecg.html#ecg-peaks).

# Find peaks
peaks, info = nk.ecg_peaks(data["ECG"], sampling_rate=100)

# *Note: It is critical that you specify the correct sampling rate of your signal throughout many processing functions, as this allows NeuroKit to have a time reference.*

# This produces two elements, `peaks` which is a DataFrame of same length as the input signal in which occurences of R-peaks are marked with 1 in a list of zeros. `info` is a dictionary of the sample points at which these R-peaks occur. 
#
# HRV is the temporal variation between consecutive heartbeats (**RR intervals**). Here, we will use `peaks` i.e. occurrences of the heartbeat peaks, as the input argument in the following HRV functions to extract the indices. 

# ## Time-Domain Analysis

# First, let's extract the time-domain indices.

# Extract clean EDA and SCR features
hrv_time = nk.hrv_time(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_time

# These features include the RMSSD (square root of the mean of the sum of successive differences between adjacent RR intervals), MeanNN (mean of RR intervals) so on and so forth. You can also visualize the distribution of R-R intervals by specifying `show=True` in [hrv_time()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-time).

# ## Frequency-Domain Analysis

# Now, let's extract the frequency domain features, which involve extracting for example the spectral power density pertaining to different frequency bands. Again, you can visualize the power across frequency bands by specifying `show=True` in [hrv_frequency()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-frequency).

hrv_freq = nk.hrv_frequency(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True, normalize=True)
hrv_freq

# ## Non-Linear Domain Analysis

# Now, let's compute the non-linear indices with [hrv_nonlinear()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-nonlinear).

hrv_nonlinear = nk.hrv_nonlinear(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_nonlinear

# This will produce a Poincaré plot which plots each RR interval against the next successive one.
#
# Note that there exist many more [**complexity indices**](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/complexity.html), that are available in NeuroKit2, and that could be applied to HRV. The ``hrv_nonlinear()`` function only includes the most commonly used indices.

# ## All Domains

# Finally, if you'd like to extract HRV indices from all three domains, you can simply input `peaks` into [hrv()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html), where you can specify `show=True` to visualize the combination of plots depicting the RR intervals distribution, power spectral density for frequency domains, and the poincare scattergram.

hrv_indices = nk.hrv(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_indices

# Heart-rate variability indices for a 5-minute resting ECG recording

## Objective

From the supplied 5-minute resting physiological recording, compute the complete set of heart-rate-variability (HRV) indices — time-domain, frequency-domain and non-linear-domain — that the analysis pipeline defined by **NeuroKit2 0.2.13** (the versioned reference preset for this task) produces from R-peaks detected in the ECG channel. The requested results are the 95 HRV index values listed under "Required output" below.

## Supplied input

- `input/bio_resting_5min_100hz.csv` — a text CSV with a header row `ECG,PPG,RSP` and one row per sample of a 5-minute recording acquired at 100 Hz (three columns: ECG, PPG, respiration). Only the **ECG** column is used by this analysis; PPG and RSP are present but unused.

## Method (conventional steps identified by the reference preset)

1. **R-peak detection** — on the ECG column *exactly as supplied* (no separate ECG-cleaning step is part of this analysis, and no artifact correction is applied), using NeuroKit2 0.2.13's default peak-detection method (`ecg_peaks` with `method="neurokit"`, `correct_artifacts=False`), sampling rate 100 Hz.
2. **HRV computation from the resulting R-peak series**, sampling rate 100 Hz, in all three domains exactly as defined by NeuroKit2 0.2.13's `hrv_time`, `hrv_frequency` and `hrv_nonlinear`:
   - **Time domain:** standard NN-interval statistics (mean, SD, RMSSD, pNNx, histogram indices, etc.), with NN intervals in **milliseconds**.
   - **Frequency domain:** RR series interpolated at 100 Hz; power spectral density estimated by the Welch method and **normalized by its maximum value** before band integration (as in the source's `normalize=True`); band edges: ultra-low 0–0.0033 Hz, very-low 0.0033–0.04 Hz, low 0.04–0.15 Hz, high 0.15–0.4 Hz, very-high 0.4–0.5 Hz; plus total power (TP), LF/HF ratio, normalized LF (LFn = LF/TP), normalized HF (HFn = HF/TP) and LnHF. Band powers are unitless (relative power on the normalized PSD).
   - **Non-linear domain:** Poincaré indices (SD1/SD2 and asymmetric variants), CSI/CVI, DFA and multifractal-DFA exponents, sample/approximate/fuzzy/multiscale entropies, Shannon entropy, and the remaining indices produced by `hrv_nonlinear` (symbolic dynamics with equal-probability 4-level coding, etc.).

Using NeuroKit2 0.2.13 directly is permitted (a compatible environment is available), but any tool is acceptable provided the requested quantities are the ones defined by this preset. Do not change the peak-detection method, artifact-correction setting, band edges, PSD method, normalization rule or sampling rate — these define the quantities being requested.

## Required output

A single file `outputs/hrv_indices.csv`: header row with the metric names below, one data row with the value for each metric. Column order is free — values are identified by column name. Metrics that are undefined for this recording (undefined per the reference method) must be left as empty fields. All 95 columns must be present:

Time domain: `HRV_MeanNN`, `HRV_SDNN`, `HRV_SDANN1`, `HRV_SDNNI1`, `HRV_SDANN2`, `HRV_SDNNI2`, `HRV_SDANN5`, `HRV_SDNNI5`, `HRV_RMSSD`, `HRV_SDSD`, `HRV_CVNN`, `HRV_CVSD`, `HRV_MedianNN`, `HRV_MadNN`, `HRV_MCVNN`, `HRV_IQRNN`, `HRV_SDRMSSD`, `HRV_Prc20NN`, `HRV_Prc80NN`, `HRV_pNN50`, `HRV_pNN20`, `HRV_MinNN`, `HRV_MaxNN`, `HRV_HTI`, `HRV_TINN`.

Frequency domain: `HRV_ULF`, `HRV_VLF`, `HRV_LF`, `HRV_HF`, `HRV_VHF`, `HRV_TP`, `HRV_LFHF`, `HRV_LFn`, `HRV_HFn`, `HRV_LnHF`.

Non-linear domain: `HRV_SD1`, `HRV_SD2`, `HRV_SD1SD2`, `HRV_S`, `HRV_CSI`, `HRV_CVI`, `HRV_CSI_Modified`, `HRV_PIP`, `HRV_IALS`, `HRV_PSS`, `HRV_PAS`, `HRV_GI`, `HRV_SI`, `HRV_AI`, `HRV_PI`, `HRV_C1d`, `HRV_C1a`, `HRV_SD1d`, `HRV_SD1a`, `HRV_C2d`, `HRV_C2a`, `HRV_SD2d`, `HRV_SD2a`, `HRV_Cd`, `HRV_Ca`, `HRV_SDNNd`, `HRV_SDNNa`, `HRV_DFA_alpha1`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Width`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Peak`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Mean`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Max`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Delta`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Asymmetry`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Fluctuation`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha1_Increment`, `HRV_DFA_alpha2`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Width`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Peak`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Mean`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Max`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Delta`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Asymmetry`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Fluctuation`, `HRV_MFDFA_alpha2_Increment`, `HRV_ApEn`, `HRV_SampEn`, `HRV_ShanEn`, `HRV_FuzzyEn`, `HRV_MSEn`, `HRV_CMSEn`, `HRV_RCMSEn`, `HRV_CD`, `HRV_HFD`, `HRV_KFD`, `HRV_LZC`, `HRV_Symbolic_EqualProb4_0V`, `HRV_Symbolic_EqualProb4_1V`, `HRV_Symbolic_EqualProb4_2LV`, `HRV_Symbolic_EqualProb4_2UV`.

(These columns exactly cover the notebook's per-domain and combined results: the notebook's three domain tables are column subsets of this one table for the same peak series and the same parameters.)

# # Heart Rate Variability (HRV)

# NeuroKit2 is the most comprehensive package when it comes to HRV indices, and this example shows how to use NeuroKit2 to compute heart rate variability (HRV) indices in the time-, frequency-, and non-linear domain.
#
# For a comprehensive review of the most up-to-date HRV indices, a discussion of their significance in psychology, and a step-by-step guide for HRV analysis using **NeuroKit2**, the [Heart Rate Variability in Psychology: A Review of HRV Indices and an Analysis Tutorial](https://doi.org/10.3390/s21123998) paper is a good place to start. 

# ## Compute HRV features

# Load the NeuroKit package
import neurokit2 as nk

# Note: this cell is hidden using the "remove-input" tag
# Make bigger images
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# --- Offline input adaptation (environment-only; no scientific change) ---
# The original notebook relies on nk.data() fetching its example dataset from
# https://raw.githubusercontent.com/neuropsychology/NeuroKit/master/data/ .
# The exact dataset file is staged at /inputs/ so the offline reference can
# read identical bytes through the unchanged nk.data() code path.
_orig_pd_read_csv = nk.pd.read_csv


def _offline_read_csv(path, *args, **kwargs):
    _nk_data_prefix = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/neuropsychology/NeuroKit/master/data/"
    if isinstance(path, str) and path.startswith(_nk_data_prefix):
        return _orig_pd_read_csv("/inputs/" + path[len(_nk_data_prefix):], *args, **kwargs)
    return _orig_pd_read_csv(path, *args, **kwargs)


nk.pd.read_csv = _offline_read_csv


plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = [15, 5]
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 14

# ## Download Dataset

# First, let's download the resting rate data (sampled at 100Hz) using `nk.data()`.

data = nk.data("bio_resting_5min_100hz")
data.head()  # Print first 5 rows

# You can see that it consists of three different signals, pertaining to ECG, PPG (an alternative determinant of heart rate as compared to ECG), and RSP (respiration). Now, let's extract the ECG signal in the shape of a vector (i.e., a one-dimensional array), and find the peaks using [ecg_peaks()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/ecg.html#ecg-peaks).

# Find peaks
peaks, info = nk.ecg_peaks(data["ECG"], sampling_rate=100)

# *Note: It is critical that you specify the correct sampling rate of your signal throughout many processing functions, as this allows NeuroKit to have a time reference.*

# This produces two elements, `peaks` which is a DataFrame of same length as the input signal in which occurences of R-peaks are marked with 1 in a list of zeros. `info` is a dictionary of the sample points at which these R-peaks occur. 
#
# HRV is the temporal variation between consecutive heartbeats (**RR intervals**). Here, we will use `peaks` i.e. occurrences of the heartbeat peaks, as the input argument in the following HRV functions to extract the indices. 

# ## Time-Domain Analysis

# First, let's extract the time-domain indices.

# Extract clean EDA and SCR features
hrv_time = nk.hrv_time(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_time

# These features include the RMSSD (square root of the mean of the sum of successive differences between adjacent RR intervals), MeanNN (mean of RR intervals) so on and so forth. You can also visualize the distribution of R-R intervals by specifying `show=True` in [hrv_time()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-time).

# ## Frequency-Domain Analysis

# Now, let's extract the frequency domain features, which involve extracting for example the spectral power density pertaining to different frequency bands. Again, you can visualize the power across frequency bands by specifying `show=True` in [hrv_frequency()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-frequency).

hrv_freq = nk.hrv_frequency(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True, normalize=True)
hrv_freq

# ## Non-Linear Domain Analysis

# Now, let's compute the non-linear indices with [hrv_nonlinear()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html#hrv-nonlinear).

hrv_nonlinear = nk.hrv_nonlinear(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_nonlinear

# This will produce a Poincaré plot which plots each RR interval against the next successive one.
#
# Note that there exist many more [**complexity indices**](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/complexity.html), that are available in NeuroKit2, and that could be applied to HRV. The ``hrv_nonlinear()`` function only includes the most commonly used indices.

# ## All Domains

# Finally, if you'd like to extract HRV indices from all three domains, you can simply input `peaks` into [hrv()](https://neuropsychology.github.io/NeuroKit/functions/hrv.html), where you can specify `show=True` to visualize the combination of plots depicting the RR intervals distribution, power spectral density for frequency domains, and the poincare scattergram.

hrv_indices = nk.hrv(peaks, sampling_rate=100, show=True)
hrv_indices


import os

os.makedirs("/work/outputs", exist_ok=True)

hrv_time.to_csv("/work/outputs/hrv_time.csv", index=False)
hrv_freq.to_csv("/work/outputs/hrv_freq.csv", index=False)
hrv_nonlinear.to_csv("/work/outputs/hrv_nonlinear.csv", index=False)
hrv_indices.to_csv("/work/outputs/hrv_indices.csv", index=False)
